source_evidence.anchor: Introduction paragraph defining SR_{p,r}, p, r, and u_p
source_evidence.observation: The paper denotes limited-precision stochastic rounding by SR_{p,r}; p-1 is the number of fraction bits in the destination format, r is the number of random bits, ideal SR_p corresponds to r=infinity, and u_p := 2^(1-p).

Lemma 2.1 states P(|X-E(X)| <= alpha sqrt(V(X))) >= 1-1/alpha^2 for finite expectation and variance and alpha>0. Definition 2.2 defines sequential mean independence by E(X_k | X_0,...,X_{k-1})=E(X_k).

The arithmetic is a normalized precision-p binary floating-point system. The unit roundoff is u_p=2^(1-p), and the standard relative-error model for stochastic rounding is fl_p(x op y)=(x op y)(1+delta) with |delta| bounded by u_p.

The construction first represents the exact input with p+r binary digits using fl_{p+r}. The text describes truncation as the default and notes that directed alternatives satisfy fl_{p+r}(x)=x(1+beta), |beta|<=u_{p+r}=2^(1-p-r).

SR_{p,r}(x) selects the adjacent p-bit upper value with probability q_r(x)=(fl_{p+r}(x)-floor_p(x))/ulp_p(x), and otherwise selects the adjacent lower value. Both SR_{p,r} and ideal SR_p output p-bit results. E(SR_{p,r}(x))=fl_{p+r}(x), so for SR_{p,r}(x)=x(1+delta), E(delta)=beta=(fl_{p+r}(x)-x)/x.

A single limited-precision stochastic-rounding error satisfies V(delta)<=u_p^2/4. Lemma 3.2 gives E(delta_k | delta_1,...,delta_{k-1})=beta_k; when the exact operation result is zero, delta_k and beta_k are both set to zero.
For k>=2, beta_k depends on earlier random rounding errors and is therefore itself random despite arising from deterministic fl_{p+r}; nevertheless E(beta_k)=E(delta_k).

For alpha_k=delta_k-beta_k, the alpha sequence is mean independent with E(alpha_k | alpha_1,...,alpha_{k-1})=E(alpha_k)=0. Products of (1+delta_k) decompose exactly into the corresponding product of (1+alpha_k) plus B_i, with |B_i|<=gamma_{n-i+1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-i+1}(u_p).

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Lemma 3.10 and opening of section 4
source_evidence.observation: The proof uses the pathwise bounds |alpha_k|<=u_p and |beta_k|<=u_{p+r}. Section 4 says the probabilistic bounds combine Lemma 3.10 with either martingale methods or the variance bound of external reference [11, Lemma 3.1] and Lemma 2.1.

For a in R^n, y=sum_{i=1}^n a_i and kappa(a)=(sum_i |a_i|)/|sum_i a_i|. The algorithm sets hat{s}_1=a_1 and hat{s}_k=SR_{p,r}(hat{s}_{k-1}+a_k) for k=2,...,n, with hat{y}=hat{s}_n. It yields hat{y}=sum_i a_i product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+delta_{k-1}). The exact error function is gamma_m(u)=(1+u)^m-1; the displayed expansion mu+O(u^2) is stated only for mu much less than 1.

With I_i={k in N : max{i,2}<=k<=n}, the product containing delta_{k-1} is replaced by the product containing alpha_{k-1} plus B_i. Algebraically hat{y}-y=M+A, where M=sum_i a_i(product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+alpha_{k-1})-1) and A=sum_i a_i B_i; equation (4.8) applies the triangle inequality to obtain |hat{y}-y|<=|M|+|A|.

Equation (4.10) gives the pathwise bound |A|<=(sum_i |a_i|)[gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)]. Theorem 4.3 states that for every 0<lambda<1, with probability at least 1-lambda, |hat{y}-y|/|y| <= kappa(a)[sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda)+gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)]. Its proof obtains |M|<=(sum_i |a_i|)sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda) with the same probability.

binders: Inherited before Theorem 4.3: a is a fixed vector in R^n and y=sum_{i=1}^n a_i; n is the dimension used by the recursive algorithm. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: section 4.1 and equation (4.1).)

Inherited: p is the destination precision and r is the positive number of random bits used by SR_{p,r}; u_p=2^(1-p) and u_{p+r}=2^(1-p-r). (PDF pp. 3 and 6, printed B1229 and B1232, anchors: introductory notation and paragraph preceding Definition 2.9.)
Explicit in Theorem 4.3: lambda is universally quantified after the summation problem and algorithm have been fixed, with 0<lambda<1. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: Theorem 4.3.)

Generated along the computation: delta_1,...,delta_{n-1} are the SR_{p,r} relative errors, beta_j are their corresponding fl_{p+r} errors, and alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j. (PDF pp. 13-14, printed B1239-B1240, anchors: equations (4.4)-(4.5) and proof leading to (4.8).)
hypotheses: The selected algorithm is left-to-right recursive summation: hat{s}_1=a_1 and hat{s}_k=SR_{p,r}(hat{s}_{k-1}+a_k) for k=2,...,n; hat{y}=hat{s}_n. The exact recurrence is s_1=a_1, s_k=s_{k-1}+a_k, and y=s_n. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: recursive-summation table.)
Each rounded addition has hat{s}_k=(hat{s}_{k-1}+a_k)(1+delta_{k-1}) with |delta_{k-1}|<=u_p. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: recursive-summation table and paragraph following (4.4).)

The centered errors alpha_j are mean independent, have zero conditional and unconditional means, and satisfy |alpha_j|<=u_p. Full independence of the delta_j or alpha_j is not assumed. (PDF pp. 11-12 and 15, printed B1237-B1238 and B1241, anchors: Lemma 3.10, its proof, and proof of Theorem 4.3.)

The corresponding beta_j errors satisfy |beta_j|<=u_{p+r}; for later operations they may depend on the previous random path. (PDF pp. 9 and 12, printed B1235 and B1238, anchors: Remark 3.4 and proof of Lemma 3.10.)

The finite-expectation and finite-variance conditions needed by Bienayme-Chebyshev are inherited through the bounded-error construction; Theorem 4.3 does not restate them separately. (PDF pp. 4 and 15, printed B1230 and B1241, anchors: Lemma 2.1 and proof of Theorem 4.3.)

For the displayed relative error and kappa(a) to be defined, y=sum_i a_i must be nonzero, although this is not explicitly included as a theorem hypothesis. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.2) and Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11).)
conclusions: For every 0<lambda<1, P(|hat{y}-y|/|y| <= kappa(a)[sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda)+gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)]) >= 1-lambda. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11).)
The probabilistic component obeys |M| <= (sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|)sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda) with probability at least 1-lambda. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: equation (4.12).)
The finite-r component obeys the pathwise bound |A| <= (sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|)[gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p)]. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: equation (4.10).)
definitions_and_conventions: y=sum_{i=1}^n a_i is the exact real sum, whereas hat{y}=hat{s}_n is the result of the stated limited-precision stochastic-rounding recurrence. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchors: equations (4.1) and (4.4).)
kappa(a)=(sum_{i=1}^n |a_i|)/|sum_{i=1}^n a_i|. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: equation (4.2).)
gamma_m(u)=(1+u)^m-1 exactly. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: equation (4.3).)

SR_{p,r}(x) is a Bernoulli choice between the adjacent p-bit floating-point neighbors of x, with upper-neighbor probability based on fl_{p+r}(x). (PDF p. 7, printed B1233, anchor: Definition 2.9 and equation (2.6).)

For the summation path, beta_{k-1} is the relative error produced by applying fl_{p+r} to the exact intermediate hat{s}_{k-1}+a_k, and alpha_{k-1}=delta_{k-1}-beta_{k-1}. (PDF pp. 13-14, printed B1239-B1240, anchors: equation (4.5) and proof of Theorem 4.2.)

For I_i={k in N : max{i,2}<=k<=n}, B_i is defined by product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+delta_{k-1})=product_{k=max{i,2}}^n(1+alpha_{k-1})+B_i. (PDF pp. 11 and 14, printed B1237 and B1240, anchors: Lemma 3.10 equation (3.8) and application in (4.8).)
implicit_context: The theorem appears inside a section introduced as analyzing vectors of floating-point numbers, while section 4.1 formally begins with a in R^n. No separate input-rounding stage is included. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed B1238-B1239, anchors: opening of section 4 and opening of section 4.1.)

The probability is over the sequence of Bernoulli choices made by SR_{p,r} along the single recursive computation path. (PDF pp. 7-9 and 13, printed B1233-B1235 and B1239, anchors: Definition 2.9, Lemma 3.2, and recursive-summation recurrence.)

The confidence statement is pointwise for the already fixed input a and arithmetic parameters; it is not a simultaneous assertion over all inputs or all lambda. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: opening of section 4.1 and Theorem 4.3.)

The proof imports the variance estimate from external reference [11, Lemma 3.1], but the present PDF exposes the resulting specialized estimate completely as equation (4.12). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: paragraph before Theorem 4.3 and its proof.)
statement.algorithm_linkage: Theorem 4.3 is tied specifically to the computed product representation (4.4) of left-to-right recursive summation under limited-precision SR_{p,r}. It is not stated for pairwise summation, compensated summation, arbitrary parenthesization, ideal SR_p except as the r-to-infinity limit, or a generic sequence of additions. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equations (4.1)-(4.4) and Theorem 4.3.)
numerical_model: The destination is a normalized binary floating-point system with precision p, and stochastic operations use the standard relative-error model with unit roundoff u_p=2^(1-p). (PDF pp. 3 and 5, printed B1229 and B1231, anchors: introductory notation and equations (2.2)-(2.4).)

Limited-precision SR_{p,r} uses only p+r bits to form its Bernoulli probability and returns a p-bit result; its expected rounded value is fl_{p+r}(x), not x. (PDF p. 7, printed B1233, anchors: Definition 2.9, Remark 2.10, and equation (3.1).)

The finite-r error is represented by beta and the centered error by alpha=delta-beta. The alpha sequence, rather than the original delta sequence, has the zero-mean conditional structure used in Theorem 4.3. (PDF pp. 11 and 15, printed B1237 and B1241, anchors: Lemma 3.10 and proof of Theorem 4.3.)

Although equation (3.2) gives the single-rounding estimate V(delta)<=u_p^2/4, the bound printed in Theorem 4.3 is exactly sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda), with no displayed factor 1/2. (PDF pp. 8 and 15, printed B1234 and B1241, anchors: equation (3.2) and equations (4.11)-(4.12).)
error_notions: The primary error notion is scalar forward relative error |hat{y}-y|/|y|. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: equation (4.11).)

M is the centered product-error contribution generated by alpha, while A collects all product terms containing at least one finite-r beta contribution through B_i. A may be path dependent, but equation (4.10) bounds it deterministically for every path. (PDF pp. 11, 14, and 15, printed B1237, B1240, and B1241, anchors: Lemma 3.10 and equations (4.8), (4.10).)

The final forward-error bound is the sum of a high-probability variance term and a pathwise finite-r remainder term, multiplied by the summation condition number kappa(a). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: equations (4.10)-(4.12).)
norms: All displayed output, M, A, and coefficient magnitudes use ordinary scalar absolute value. (PDF pp. 14-15, printed B1240-B1241, anchors: equations (4.8), (4.10), and (4.12).)

The coefficient scale sum_i |a_i| is the componentwise absolute sum, equivalently the vector 1-norm, although the paper expresses it as a sum rather than introducing norm notation. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.2) and equations (4.10), (4.12).)
No 2-norm, infinity norm, componentwise relative-error vector, or backward-error norm appears in Theorem 4.3. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11).)
constants_and_indexing: There are n-1 rounded additions and errors delta_1,...,delta_{n-1}; the kth addition for k=2,...,n carries delta_{k-1}. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: recursive-summation table.)
The contribution of a_i is multiplied from k=max{i,2} through n, so a_1 and a_2 both encounter all n-1 rounding factors. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: equation (4.4).)
Every gamma index in Theorem 4.3 is n-1, matching the number of rounded additions. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: equation (4.11).)
The first gamma argument in the probabilistic term is u_p^2. It is not u_{2p}, gamma_{n-1}(u_p)^2, or u_p. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: equations (4.11)-(4.12).)
The confidence parameter occurs as division by lambda inside the square root, and the success probability is at least 1-lambda. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: equation (4.11).)
The finite-r term is the difference gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p), not merely gamma_{n-1}(u_{p+r}). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: equations (4.10)-(4.11).)
higher_order_terms: The theorem uses gamma_m(u)=(1+u)^m-1 exactly and therefore retains all powers of u. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.3) and Theorem 4.3.)

The expansion gamma_m(u)=mu+O(u^2) for mu much less than 1 is explanatory context only; Theorem 4.3 neither substitutes this approximation nor appends an omitted big-O remainder. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.3) and equation (4.11).)

No small-u or (n-1)u_p much-less-than-one condition is explicitly imposed by Theorem 4.3 for its exact gamma-form bound. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.3) and theorem hypothesis.)
exceptional_values: If an exact elementary-operation result is zero, the paper's supporting Lemma 3.2 sets both delta_k and beta_k to zero, avoiding division by zero in their relative-error definitions. (PDF p. 8, printed B1234, anchor: proof of Lemma 3.2.)

The final relative error and kappa(a) are undefined when y=0; the paper does not state a y!=0 hypothesis or provide an absolute-error alternative in Theorem 4.3. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.2) and equation (4.11).)

The floating-point setup is normalized and the standard multiplicative model is assumed, but the cited passages do not explicitly discuss overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, or NaNs. Thus the theorem implicitly concerns executions for which the displayed real relative-error model remains valid. (PDF p. 5, printed B1231, anchor: section 2.2 and equation (2.4).)

undebatable_constraints: The computed value must be the output of the exact recursive SR_{p,r} algorithm in (4.4), with hat{s}_1=a_1 and one rounded addition for each k=2,...,n. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchors: recursive-summation table and equation (4.4).)
The exact comparator is y=sum_{i=1}^n a_i, and the conditioning multiplier is kappa(a)=sum_i |a_i|/|y|. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchors: equations (4.1)-(4.2).)

The centered variables are alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j; mean independence and the bound |alpha_j|<=u_p apply to alpha_j, not generally to the biased delta_j sequence. (PDF pp. 11-12 and 15, printed B1237-B1238 and B1241, anchors: Lemma 3.10 and proof of Theorem 4.3.)
The probabilistic term is exactly sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: equations (4.11)-(4.12).)
The limited-r remainder is exactly gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchors: equations (4.10)-(4.11).)
The entire bracket is multiplied by kappa(a), and the asserted probability is at least 1-lambda for every 0<lambda<1. (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: Theorem 4.3 equation (4.11).)
gamma_m(u) means the exact expression (1+u)^m-1; replacing it by mu is only an approximation and changes the theorem. (PDF p. 13, printed B1239, anchor: equation (4.3).)

The proof combines the probabilistic M estimate with the pathwise A estimate through the M+A decomposition; the finite-r term is not assigned an additional failure probability. (PDF pp. 14-15, printed B1240-B1241, anchors: equations (4.8), (4.10), and (4.12).)

The theorem is a scalar forward relative-error result and does not claim unbiasedness, backward stability, an expectation bound, or an error bound for a different summation order. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equation (4.4) and Theorem 4.3.)

ambiguities.issue: The zero exact-sum case is not covered explicitly.
ambiguities.evidence: Both kappa(a) in (4.2) and the left side of (4.11) divide by |y|, but Theorem 4.3 does not state y!=0. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: equations (4.2) and (4.11).)
ambiguities.impact: A faithful formalization must either assume y!=0, use a convention for division by zero, or formulate a separate absolute-error statement; the PDF does not choose among these.

ambiguities.issue: The minimum permitted dimension is not stated.
ambiguities.evidence: Section 4.1 says a in R^n and defines a recurrence for k=2,...,n, while Theorem 4.3 uses gamma_{n-1}; it does not say n>=1 or n>=2. (PDF pp. 13 and 15, printed B1239 and B1241, anchors: section 4.1 and equation (4.11).)
ambiguities.impact: For n=1, empty products and gamma_0 must be interpreted conventionally; alternatively, a formal statement may require n>=2. The source does not resolve this edge case.

ambiguities.issue: Input representability is not stated consistently.
ambiguities.evidence: Section 4 is introduced as analyzing vectors of floating-point numbers, but section 4.1 formally takes a in R^n, initializes hat{s}_1=a_1 exactly, and includes no input-rounding errors. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed B1238-B1239, anchors: opening of section 4 and recursive-summation table.)
ambiguities.impact: It is unclear whether every a_i is assumed representable in the p-bit system or whether exact real inputs are supplied without initial rounding. Adding input-conversion errors would be a different theorem.

ambiguities.issue: The domains of p and r are partly conveyed through bit-count semantics rather than repeated theorem binders.
ambiguities.evidence: The floating-point section says p>0, while the construction describes r as a positive integer and both quantities count bits; Theorem 4.3 does not rebind either parameter. (PDF pp. 3, 5-6, and 15, printed B1229, B1231-B1232, and B1241, anchors: introductory notation, section 2.2, paragraph preceding Definition 2.9, and Theorem 4.3.)
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should normally take p and r as positive integers, but only r is explicitly called an integer in the surrounding prose.

ambiguities.issue: The implementation of fl_{p+r} admits a noted variation.
ambiguities.evidence: The construction describes truncation to p+r bits but notes that fl_{p+r} could use another rounding mode, with directed modes retaining |beta|<=u_{p+r}; Definition 2.9 defines q_r through fl_{p+r}. (PDF pp. 6-7, printed B1232-B1233, anchors: paragraph preceding Definition 2.9 and equation (2.6).)
ambiguities.impact: Changing fl_{p+r} changes the Bernoulli probabilities and path distribution. The printed bound appears to use only the beta bound, but the operator variant should not be silently selected when reproducing the source.

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point behavior is outside the explicit model.
ambiguities.evidence: The paper defines a normalized finite-exponent system and assumes the multiplicative model (2.4), without stating conditions excluding overflow, underflow, or subnormal behavior in Theorem 4.3. (PDF p. 5 and p. 15, printed B1231 and B1241, anchors: section 2.2 and Theorem 4.3.)
ambiguities.impact: The theorem should be understood only where all operations satisfy the stated relative-error model, but the exact range-side assumptions are not enumerated.

ambiguities.issue: The complete statement of the imported variance lemma is not reproduced.
ambiguities.evidence: The proof cites external [11, Lemma 3.1] and Lemma 2.1 after stating that alpha_{k-1} are mean independent and bounded, then directly records the specialized result as (4.12). (PDF p. 15, printed B1241, anchor: proof of Theorem 4.3.)
ambiguities.impact: Equation (4.12) and hence Theorem 4.3 are unambiguous in this PDF, but any additional general hypotheses of the external lemma cannot be recovered from the cited passage alone.

contract_plain_english: Fix the left-to-right recursive sum of a=(a_1,...,a_n), computed by setting hat{s}_1=a_1 and rounding each subsequent addition with limited-precision stochastic rounding SR_{p,r}; let y=sum_i a_i and hat{y}=hat{s}_n. Split each biased rounding error delta_j into beta_j, the p+r-bit finite-r component, and alpha_j=delta_j-beta_j. The alpha_j are zero-mean and mean independent with |alpha_j|<=u_p, while all terms involving beta_j admit a pathwise product-remainder bound. Consequently, for every 0<lambda<1, with probability at least 1-lambda, |hat{y}-y|/|y| is at most kappa(a) times sqrt(gamma_{n-1}(u_p^2)/lambda)+gamma_{n-1}(u_p+u_{p+r})-gamma_{n-1}(u_p), where kappa(a)=sum_i|a_i|/|y|, u_p=2^(1-p), u_{p+r}=2^(1-p-r), and gamma_m(u)=(1+u)^m-1 exactly. The statement implicitly needs y!=0 and an execution satisfying the paper's standard relative-error model. (PDF pp. 11 and 13-15, printed B1237 and B1239-B1241, anchors: Lemma 3.10 and equations (4.1)-(4.5), (4.8), (4.10)-(4.12).)
